title: Strategic Investment under Uncertainty with First- and Second-mover Advantages

p.t: In strategically competitive industries, the first mover is often perceived to have an advantage over followers. 1 However, it is sometimes advantageous to be the second mover. For example, by observing and learning from the first mover's successes and failures, the second mover can lower its production cost and have a more e cient production technology. The ulcer-relief drug Zantac is a known successful second mover, which enjoyed lower R&D and legal compliance costs than the industry leader (Berndt, Pindyck, and Azoulay, 2003). 2 Using the oil and gas sector, a widely used example for real-option analyses, Décaire and Wittry (2022) document that "a firm's incentive to delay its investment grows with the amount of information expected to be released by its peers." This is because a firm prefers to exercise its growth option as the second mover in order to acquire information revealed by its peers' investment decisions. Décaire and Wittry (2022) conclude that "In equilibrium, a war-of-attrition regarding the timing of investment decisions among peers ensues, resulting in delays." In this paper, we develop a tractable duopoly entry model to parsimoniously capture the equilibrium implications of both the first-mover and second-mover advantages. Our model delivers the following insights. First, when the first-mover advantage dominates, firms play pure entry strategies as in Fudenberg and Tirole (1985). Second, when the second-mover advantage dominates, a firm delays its entry with the hope that its competitor enters as Leader. This is because the entry game is e↵ectively a war of attrition with Leader being the loser of the game, which is consistent with empirical findings in Décaire and Wittry (2022).

A key prediction of our model is that firms use mixed strategies to enter probabilistically for some ranges of market demand. 3 For empirical support of mixed strategies in dynamic games, see Wang (2009) who analyzes firm price-setting strategies in retail gasoline markets. An important feature of our model is the nonlinear interaction between the two types of 1 For example, being the first mover may enable a firm to establish strong brand recognition and product loyalty. Also, by entering first, a firm makes it less profitable for its competitor to enter. As a result, the competitor voluntarily waits until the total market demand rises to a higher level before entering the market. In equilibrium, Leader earns monopoly profits until Follower enters. 2 For the second-mover advantage analysis using the Zantac case, also see https://insight.kellogg. northwestern.edu/article/the_second_mover_advantage, titled "The Second-Mover Advantage," based on a marketing research article (Shankar et al., 1998), in Northwestern Kellogg's Insight. 3 Asymmetric pure-strategy equilibria also exist. We characterize these equilibria in Section 7. advantages, which generates new predictions that would have been absent in a setting with only one of the two advantages. For example, in addition to a pure-strategy entry region, our model also predicts two disconnected waiting regions as well as two disconnected mixedstrategy entry regions. One immediate implication of this five-region prediction is that a firm's market entry propensity is non-monotonic in market demand.

Our model builds on the duopoly model of Dixit and Pindyck (1994) (in Chapter 9), which features the first-mover advantage only. 4 Two ex ante identical firms, a and b, discount cash flows at the rate r > 0 and compete to enter a new product market where the demand X t follows a geometric Brownian motion (with drift µ and volatility ). Each firm can pay a fixed cost to enter the market at any time. Leader captures the entire demand until the second firm (Follower) enters. Upon entering the market, Follower takes away a half of the total market demand from Leader. 5 Thus in our model, the first-mover advantage arises from the monopoly rents that Leader enjoys before Follower enters. We make a single change to the duopoly model of Dixit and Pindyck (1994) by letting Follower's entry cost (K F ) di↵er from Leader's entry cost (K L ). When the entry-cost ratio R = K L /K F > 1, firms have a second-mover advantage. Depending on the market demand, the second-mover advantage either dominates or is dominated by the first-mover advantage. There are three Markov subgame-perfect equilibria: one symmetric equilibrium and two asymmetric equilibria. We characterize solutions in closed form for all three equilibria. In an asymmetric equilibrium, which firm is Leader and which is Follower are known at the beginning. Firms use pure strategies characterized by entry thresholds. 6 Compared with the asymmetric equilibria, the predictions of the symmetric equilibrium are much richer and the solution is much subtler. For example, probabilistic entry is an essential part of a firm's equilibrium entry strategy when R > 1. Moreover, there may exist disjoint mixed-strategy regions and disjoint waiting regions. Pure and mixed entry strategies can coexist.

Our model has five parameters: the discount rate r, drift µ and volatility , and two entry costs (K L and K F ). For a given set of (r, µ, , K L , K F ), the symmetric equilibrium solution belongs to one of the three cases: A, B, and C. In Case A where the entry-cost ratio R is so large that the second-mover advantage always dominates the first-mover advantage, firms prefer entering as Follower under all circumstances. However, without Leader there would be no Follower. Put di↵erently, while being Follower is always better than being Leader, when market demand is high a firm forgoes a large profit each period it waits. A firm takes both the waiting benefit (to capture the second-mover advantage) and the waiting cost (to forgo a large profit) into account when making its entry decision. In equilibrium, when market demand is high, both firms must probabilistically enter at the same rate per unit of time. But how do we determine the equilibrium entry probability (rate) for the mixed strategy? First, when using a mixed strategy, a firm must be indi↵erent between the strategies that it chooses to mix and its value is independent of its own entry rate. 7 In equilibrium, the rate at which a firm probabilistically enters is chosen to make its competitor indi↵erent between entering as Leader and waiting for another period. In our symmetric equilibrium, which we show is Markov subgame perfect, firms enter at the same rate.

When one firm becomes Leader, the other luckily becomes Follower and its value immediately jumps upward reflecting the equilibrium result that the second-mover advantage dominates in Case A. After Leader is determined, Follower solves a single-firm real-option problem by choosing its optimal entry time to obtain its market share. Follower has two entry strategies: It either enters immediately after Leader does or waits until the market demand rises further. Which strategy Follower chooses critically depends on market demand X t and the degree of the second-mover advantage measured by the entry-cost ratio R. First, what happens when market demand is very high? In this case, Follower enters immediately after Leader does because Follower's profits are high. This suggests that there exists an endogenous threshold for market demand X t , x, above which firms play mixed strategies. That is, the x x region is a probabilistic entry region. And once Leader is determined, Follower immediately enters, leaving no monopoly rents for Leader. Second, when market demand is low, firms wait for both the option value of waiting (as in standard single-firm real-option models) and the waiting-to-be-Follower (to lower its entry cost) reasons. This suggests that there exists another endogenous threshold for market demand, e x, below which firms wait. That is, the x < e x region is the waiting region. Third, what happens when market demand X t further exceeds e

x? In this scenario, the market demand X t for a single firm as a monopolist is sizeable but it is not large enough for two firms to share. It is thus not in Follower's interest to enter. Instead, Follower preserves its option value of waiting until market demand further rises. Anticipating Follower's entry strategy, both firms adopt the mixed strategy to enter probabilistically when market demand is medium. However, as market demand further rises, Follower's incentive to enter the market becomes stronger, which reduces the duration that Leader can earn monopoly rents and hence discourages firms to probabilistically enter as Leader. This suggests another threshold x, which defines a second mixed-strategy region where x 2 [e x, x]. In this region, firms probabilistically enter as Leader. Once Leader is determined, Follower waits and then enters when market demand further rises to a threshold x F that is higher than x. A firm's equilibrium entry rate (X t ) as Leader is generally not monotonic as Follower's incentive to enter increases with X t , undermining firms' ex ante incentives to enter as Leader. Finally, as market demand further rises, anticipating Follower's immediate entry, both firms wait with probability one until market demand reaches the threshold, x, above which firms play mixed strategies as we discussed earlier. The x 2 (x, x) region is a second waiting region (between the two probabilistic entry regions).

In sum, there are four regions in general for Case A where the second-mover advantage dominates: 1.) In the x < e x region, firms wait; 2.) In the x 2 [e x, x] region, firms enter probabilistically with Leader earning equilibrium monopoly rents; 3.) In the x 2 (x, x) region, firms wait; and 4.) In the x x region, firms enter probabilistically with Follower entering immediately after Leader and leaving no monopoly rents to Leader. Note that the two waiting regions and the two probabilistic entry regions alternate. Next, we turn to Case C where there is no second-mover advantage as Leader's entry cost is lower than Follower's (R  1). 8 When market demand is high, firms rush to enter and one firm is randomly selected as Leader in a way that ex ante rents that the two firms earn are equalized. There are two equilibrium regions: the waiting (for the standard real-option argument) region where x < b x L and the rushing-to-enter region (to capture the first-mover advantage) where x b x L . The endogenous threshold b x L is the turning point above which firms rush to become Leader. Finally, we are ready to analyze Case B where R is larger than one but not very large. Because Case B is the intermediate case between Case A and Case C, we expect its solution is even richer, which indeed features five regions. On one hand, similar to Case A, the secondmover advantage dominates if market demand is su ciently high, exceeding an endogenous threshold b

On the other hand, with a weaker second-mover advantage (a lower R than in Case A), the first-mover advantage dominates in the [b x L , b x F ] region, which is to the right of the (0, b x L ) waiting region. Recall that when market demand further rises above b x F , firms anticipate Follower's stronger incentive to enter, which implies a shorter monopoly duration and lower monopoly rents for Leader, discouraging their ex ante incentives to enter as Leader. This explains why two firms compete to enter in the [b x L , b x F ] region but enter probabilistically in the (b x F , x] region. In sum, Case B in general features five equilibrium regions, as summarized in Figure 1. 9 Related Literature. Our paper contributes to the strategic real-options literature. 10 This literature has focused on the first-mover advantage. By introducing the entry-cost wedge between Leader and Follower, we generate new predictions that models with only the first-mover advantage cannot capture. For example, we show that a model with just five parameters (discount rate, drift and volatility of market demand, and two entry costs) can generate a fiveregion solution due to the interaction between the first-and second-mover advantages. Grenadier (1996) studies real-estate redevelopment by incorporating the following feature into the duopoly real-option model in Chapter 9 of Dixit and Pindyck (1994): When Leader starts its redevelopment, Follower loses a fraction of its rents from its existing businesses.

While both our and his models generate a non-monotonic firm entry propensity with respect to market demand, the mechanisms are di↵erent in the two models. In our model, the nonmonotonicity arises from the strategic interaction induced by the second-mover advantage considerations. In contrast, there is no second-mover advantage in Grenadier (1996). Therefore, di↵erent from our model, there are no mixed strategies and no interaction between the first-mover and second-mover advantages in Grenadier (1996). Appendix B provides a detailed comparison between the Grenadier (1996) model and our model. Grenadier (2002) and Back and Paulsen (2009) analyze continuous-time oligopoly capitalaccumulation games. They show that competition causes firms to speed up their investment rates. Di↵erent from them, the second-mover advantage plays a crucial role and also firm entry is non-monotonic in market demand in our model. Also the underlying single-firm monopoly problem in their models is a singular-control problem and that is why investment is characterized by a running maximum capital stock. 11 In contrast, the underlying singlefirm monopoly problem for our model is an optimal stopping-time problem and that is why investment is characterized by an endogenous cuto↵ threshold. In sum, the economic insights and mathematical analysis of our model are complementary to but quite di↵erent from those in Grenadier (2002) and Back and Paulsen (2009). Whether an equilibrium is subgame perfect or not is a key issue in the real-option games literature. Back and Paulsen (2009) show that the perfectly competitive outcome, produced by closed-loop strategies that are firms' mutually best responses, is Markov subgame perfect in their capital accumulation game model. Similarly, we show that the equilibria in our model are Markov subgame perfect. 12 Lambrecht (2001) develops a duopoly exit model in a real-option setting with two ex ante heterogeneous firms and studies pure-strategy equilibria. 13 In contrast, we analyze how ex ante identical firms become ex post heterogeneous via their market entry decisions and characterize pure-strategy and mixed-strategy equilibria as well as hybrid-strategy equilibria, which feature state-contingent pure and mixed strategies. In Dai, Jiang, and Wang (2023), we study equilibrium capital structure and firm default by incorporating firm reputation into a duopoly setting, and show that there exists a symmetric mixed strategy equilibrium.

The second-mover advantage part of our model mechanism is related to but di↵erent from the classic war-of-attrition argument. 14 First, while classic attrition games are about firm exit, our model is about firm entry and thus has to be solved via backward induction. Second, while firm payo↵s in war-of-attrition games are often exogenous (Levin, 2004), they are endogenous in our model. This is because Leader's payo↵ depends on Follower's equilibrium strategy and contains an option-value component. Importantly, our paper focuses on the interaction between the first-and the second-mover advantages, which induces the coexistence of statedependent mixed and pure strategies in our duopoly model, absent in standard war-of-attrition models. Finally, a firm's entry propensity is not monotonic in market demand unlike in warof-attrition models. Our model is also related to Chamley and Gale (1994) and Grenadier (1999), in which firms delay entry timing in anticipation of information spillover from peers' decisions. Unlike these social-learning-based models, our model features entry-cost savings for the second mover generating the coexistence of state-contingent first-mover and second-mover advantages. There is also a growing literature that integrates industrial organization considerations into asset pricing models. Dou, Ji, and Wu (2022) extend the standard Lucas-tree asset pricing model to allow for endogenous strategic competition. Chen, Dou, Guo, and Ji (2022) study how strategic competition and financial distress dynamically interact.

Next, we turn to the key assumption of our model on firm entry costs. We assume that Leader incurs a larger entry cost than Follower does as Leader may have to pay additional innovation and marketing costs, learn about a new product market, and work with local governments in the new markets. Follower can save some of the costs by observing Leader's actions, learning from Leader's experiences and mistakes, and even possibly imitating Leader's success and copying Leader's strategies. We capture the second-mover advantage by letting Follower's entry cost be lower than Leader's. Let K L > 0 and K F > 0 denote the entry cost that Leader and Follower have to pay at their entry time ⌧ L and ⌧ F , respectively. We analyze how a firm optimally takes into account both the first-mover and the secondmover advantages when deciding its entry decision in a classic duopoly real-option framework (McDonald and Siegel, 1986; Dixit and Pindyck, 1994). Our general model solution (Subcase B 1 ) features five regions, defined by four endogenous cuto↵ values (b x L , b x F , x, x) in ascending order. In addition to the option-value of waiting region where x 2 (0, b x L ) and the competingto-enter region where x 2 [b x L , b x F ] (due to the first-move advantage) as in Dixit and Pindyck (1994), there are three new regions in the x > b x F domain where the second-mover advantage dominates: 1.) in the x 2 (b x F , x] region, firms enter probabilistically and Leader earns monopoly rents until Follower enters; 2.) in the x x region, firms enter probabilistically with no equilibrium monopoly rents for Leader; and 3.) in the x 2 (x, x) region between the two probabilistic entry regions, firms wait. Our model generates new quantitative and testable predictions. For example, firm entry is non-monotonic with respect to market demand and can occur either in clusters or sequentially. Also in contrast to the classic real-option model's prediction, a firm's (pre-entry) option value can be concave in market demand x and decrease with market volatility in the probabilistic entry region (with monopoly rents) due to the interactive e↵ect between imperfect competition and the second-mover advantage.

To sharpen the key mechanism of duopoly entry games, we have purposefully chosen a minimalistic setting. A firm has complete information about its competitor's cost structure and type. One important extension that we plan to pursue is to incorporate the e↵ects of reputation as in Kreps and Wilson (1982), Milgrom and Roberts (1982), and Abreu and Gul (2000) into our duopoly entry game. Another interesting extension of our model is to grant the first mover with monopoly rents for some periods to capture industrial policies, e.g., patent protection for newly developed drugs. Indeed, a key reason for patent protection is to encourage firm innovation and entry, consistent with our duopoly model's excessive entry delay prediction caused by the second-mover advantage.
